claim: String-pulling by rodents is a behavior in which animals make rhythmical body, head, and bilateral forearm as well as skilled hand movements to spontaneously reel in a string.
source: String-pulling by rodents is a behavior in which animals make rhythmical body, head, and bilateral forearm as well as skilled hand movements to spontaneously reel in a string.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract describing the string-pulling behavior.

claim: Variations of string-pulling behavior are observed in over 160 species of animals including birds, bees, rodents and primates and humans.
source: Variations of the behavior are observed in over 160 species of animals including birds, bees, rodents and primates and humans (Jacobs and Osvath, 2015; Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jacobs and Osvath, 2015 and Singh et al., 2019.

claim: The string-pulling task has been used to assess cognitive function, motivation, brain and spinal cord injury and disease consequences and work/reward relations in animals.
source: The task has been used to assess cognitive function, motivation, brain and spinal cord injury and disease consequences and work/reward relations in animals and as a therapy and exercise tool in humans.
evidence: This statement describes established uses of the task, drawing from general knowledge in the field.

claim: Mice will spontaneously reel in a string, but the behavior becomes more reliable when reinforced by a food reward attached to the string.
source: Mice will even spontaneously reel in a string, but the behavior becomes more reliable when reinforced by a food reward attached to the string (Laidre, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Laidre, 2008.

claim: String-pulling movement is an on-line act, guided by sensory information from snout vibrissae.
source: The movement is an on-line act, guided by sensory information from snout vibrissea, and features four hand shaping movements for grasping and releasing the string, and five arm movements for retreiving and advancing the string that are similar in mice, rats, and humans (Blackwell et al., 2018a; Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blackwell et al., 2018a and Singh et al., 2019.

claim: String-pulling features four hand shaping movements for grasping and releasing the string, and five arm movements for retrieving and advancing the string that are similar in mice, rats, and humans.
source: The movement is an on-line act, guided by sensory information from snout vibrissea, and features four hand shaping movements for grasping and releasing the string, and five arm movements for retreiving and advancing the string that are similar in mice, rats, and humans (Blackwell et al., 2018a; Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blackwell et al., 2018a and Singh et al., 2019.

claim: The reaching/grasping movements of string-pulling resemble the movements of reach-to-eat movements displayed by rodents in other tasks, including the staircase and the single-pellet reaching task.
source: The reaching/grasping movements of string-pulling resemble the movements of reach-to-eat movements displayed by rodents in other tasks, including the staircase (Dunnett, 2010) and the single-pellet reaching task (Whishaw, 1996) but additionally both hands can be assessed concurrently and many reach movements can be collected rapidly.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dunnett, 2010 and Whishaw, 1996.

claim: In string-pulling, both hands can be assessed concurrently and many reach movements can be collected rapidly.
source: The reaching/grasping movements of string-pulling resemble the movements of reach-to-eat movements displayed by rodents in other tasks, including the staircase (Dunnett, 2010) and the single-pellet reaching task (Whishaw, 1996) but additionally both hands can be assessed concurrently and many reach movements can be collected rapidly.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the advantages of string-pulling over other tasks, based on the authors' knowledge and inference.

claim: The organized structure of string-pulling makes the task useful for investigating sensory, motor, cognitive and social learning, as well as studying pathophysiology of motor deficits in animal models of motor disorders.
source: The organized structure of string-pulling makes the task useful for investigating sensory, motor, cognitive and social learning, as well as studying pathophysiology of motor deficits in animal models of motor disorders (Blackwell et al., 2018c).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blackwell et al., 2018c.

claim: The string-pulling task for mice has promise as an unconditioned motor task for phenotyping the growing number of transgenic mouse models of neurological and other diseases.
source: The string-pulling task for mice has promise as an unconditioned motor task for phenotyping the growing number of transgenic mouse models of neurological and other diseases but requires an analytical method for its systematic analysis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential utility of the task.

claim: Currently, most of the analysis of string-pulling is carried out with manual annotation of frames leading to low yield of experiments.
source: Currently, most of the analysis is carried out with manual annotation of frames leading to low yield of experiments.
evidence: This statement describes the current state of analysis methods, based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Automated analysis of mouse string-pulling is a useful way for obtaining an objective kinematic assessment of movements, for identifying the contributions of different body parts to string-advancement, and for gaining insights into inter hand coordination.
source: Automated analysis of mouse string-pulling is useful way for obtaining an objective kinematic assessment of movements, for identifying the contributions of different body parts to string-advancement, and for gaining insights into inter hand coordination (Whishaw, 1996; Dunnett and Brooks, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Whishaw, 1996 and Dunnett and Brooks, 2018.

claim: The toolbox features a graphical user interface for video data analysis.
source: The toolbox features a graphical user interface for video data analysis and follows the analysis framework with two major components, a global assessment of whole-body position and speed and fine kinematic assessment of movements of body, ears, nose, and hands (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the software features presented in the manuscript.

claim: The analysis framework has two major components: a global assessment of whole-body position and speed and fine kinematic assessment of movements of body, ears, nose, and hands.
source: The toolbox features a graphical user interface for video data analysis and follows the analysis framework with two major components, a global assessment of whole-body position and speed and fine kinematic assessment of movements of body, ears, nose, and hands (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis framework, supported by Figure 1 which illustrates the workflow.

claim: The software allows tracking of body, ears, nose, and forehands for estimation of kinematic parameters such as body length, body angle, head roll, head yaw, head pitch, and path and speed of hand movements.
source: Based on image-segmentation and heuristic algorithms for object tracking, the software also allows tracking of body, ears, nose, and forehands for estimation of kinematic parameters such as body length, body angle, head roll, head yaw, head pitch, and path and speed of hand movements.
evidence: This is a description of the software capabilities presented in the manuscript.

claim: White mice have larger variation in positions of the body compared to Black mice.
source: We demonstrate phenotyping differences in the motor behavior of C57BL/6 (Back) and Swiss Webster (White) mice and present findings that White mice have larger variation in positions of the body, larger body speed but smaller reach-cycle time of string-pulling motion as compared to Black mice.
evidence: This finding is based on experimental data comparing the two mouse strains.

claim: White mice have larger body speed compared to Black mice.
source: We demonstrate phenotyping differences in the motor behavior of C57BL/6 (Back) and Swiss Webster (White) mice and present findings that White mice have larger variation in positions of the body, larger body speed but smaller reach-cycle time of string-pulling motion as compared to Black mice.
evidence: This finding is based on experimental data comparing the two mouse strains.

claim: White mice have smaller reach-cycle time of string-pulling motion compared to Black mice.
source: We demonstrate phenotyping differences in the motor behavior of C57BL/6 (Back) and Swiss Webster (White) mice and present findings that White mice have larger variation in positions of the body, larger body speed but smaller reach-cycle time of string-pulling motion as compared to Black mice.
evidence: This finding is based on experimental data comparing the two mouse strains.

claim: The spatial entropy of the mean frames was larger for White compared to Black mice (p=0.0092, effect size = 2.157).
source: The spatial entropy of the mean frames was larger for White compared to Black mice (p=0.0092, effect size = 2.157, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 2E.

claim: The mean frame of White mice had more random values as compared to Black mice owing to larger number of distinct positions.
source: This suggests that the mean frame of White mice had more random values as compared to Black mice owing to larger number of distinct positions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial entropy finding, based on inference from the data.

claim: The means of skewness, temporal entropy, and HiFD were significantly larger for White compared to Black mice.
source: The means of skewness, temporal entropy, and HiFD were significantly larger for White compared to Black mice (individual Student's t-tests, p<0.001, p=0.008, and p=0.007 with the following effect sizes: 4.035, 2.219, and 2.737, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: Kurtosis values were significantly larger for Black mice compared to White mice (p=0.009, effect size = 2.138).
source: The opposite was the case for Kurtosis values (p=0.009, effect size = 2.138).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: The spatial entropy and sharpness for the standard deviation frames were significantly larger for the White compared to Black mice (p=0.023 and p=0.017 with effect sizes: 1.825 and 1.910, respectively).
source: The measures of spatial entropy and sharpness for the standard deviation frames were significantly larger for the White compared to Black mice (p=0.023 and p=0.017 with the following effect sizes: 1.825 and 1.910, respectively Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 3I.

claim: The spatial entropy of HiFD frame was significantly larger for the Black compared to White mice (p=0.023, effect size = 1.776).
source: The spatial entropy of HiFD frame was significantly larger for the Black compared to White mice (p=0.023, effect size = 1.776).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: The sharpness of the Fano factor, temporal entropy, and HiFD frames was significantly larger for the Black compared to White mice (p=0.007, p<0.001, and p=0.007 with effect sizes: 2.261, 3.305, 2.580, respectively).
source: Finally, the sharpness of the Fano factor, temporal entropy, and HiFD frames was significantly larger for the Black compared to White mice (p=0.007, p<0.001, and p=0.007 with the following effect size: 2.261, 3.305, 2.580, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: The CLG optical flow algorithm faithfully captured the motion dynamics of video frames.
source: The algorithm faithfully captured the motion dynamics of video frames (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is an assessment of the algorithm's performance based on visual inspection of the results shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: The mean speed for White mice was significantly larger than that for Black mice (Student's t-test, p=0.003, effect size = 2.607).
source: The mean speed for White mice was significantly larger than that for Black mice (Student's t-test, p=0.003, effect size = 2.607).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: The spatial entropy of mode frames was significantly larger for Black mice compared to White (Student's t-test, p=0.017 and effect size = 1.894).
source: These measures were not different for groups of Black and White mice except that the spatial entropy of mode frames was significantly larger for Black mice compared to White (Student's t-test, p=0.017 and effect size = 1.894) highlighting that for White mice most frequent speeds are those of hands positioned around the center of body.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data with an interpretation.

claim: White mice had faster movements than Black mice more localized on their body.
source: Overall, these results suggest that White mice had faster movements than Black mice more localized on their body.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the speed analysis results.

claim: The mean skewness (positive) and Fano factor were larger for Black compared to White mice (Student's t-test, p=0.028 and p=0.023 with effect sizes: 1.686 and 1.781, respectively).
source: The mean skewness (positive) and Fano factor were larger for Black compared to White mice (Student's t-test, p=0.028 and p=0.023 with the following effect sizes: 1.686 and 1.781, respectively) owing to smaller means (see representative mean frames in Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data with reference to Figure 4.

claim: Temporal entropy and HiFD measures were larger for White compared to Black mice (p=0.003 and p=0.008 with effect sizes: 2.700 and 2.495, respectively).
source: The opposite was true for temporal entropy and HiFD measures (p=0.003 and p=0.008 with the following effect sizes: 2.700 and 2.495, respecctively).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: The spatial entropy of PC1 of image sequence was larger for White compared to Black mice (p=0.011, effect size = 2.095).
source: For PC1s of both image sequence and speed frames, the spatial entropy, sharpness, and Hausdorff fractal dimensions of Black and White mice were similar (Student's t-test, Figure 6E), except the spatial entropy of PC1 of image sequence was larger for White compared to Black mice (p=0.011, effect size = 2.095).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 6E.

claim: The mean explained variance of PC1 of the image sequence for Black mice was significantly larger than that of White mice (p<0.0001, effect size = 6.363).
source: However, the mean explained variance of PC1 of the image sequence for Black mice was significantly larger than that of White mice compared with a Student's t-test (p<0.0001, effect size = 6.363), whereas the explained variance of PC1 of the speed frames was smaller for Black mice compared to White mice (p=0.032, effect size = 1.636).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: The explained variance of PC1 of the speed frames was smaller for Black mice compared to White mice (p=0.032, effect size = 1.636).
source: However, the mean explained variance of PC1 of the image sequence for Black mice was significantly larger than that of White mice compared with a Student's t-test (p<0.0001, effect size = 6.363), whereas the explained variance of PC1 of the speed frames was smaller for Black mice compared to White mice (p=0.032, effect size = 1.636).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: The spatial entropy as well as sharpness was larger for White mice compared to Black for Max and Min projections of ICs.
source: The spatial entropy as well as sharpness was larger for White mice compared to Black supporting results reported above (p-values for comparison of spatial entropy of Max-IC-Position and Max-IC-Speed are 0.012 and 0.011 with the following effect sizes: 2.043 and 2.091, respectively; p-value for comparison of sharpness of Max-IC-Speed is 0.034 with effect size = 1.618, for IC frames of PCs, p-values for comparison of spatial entropy of Max-IC-Position and Max-IC-Speed are 0.030 and 0.008 with the following effect sizes:1.661 and 2.204, respectively; p-value for comparison of sharpness of Max-IC-Speed is 0.025 with effect size = 1.741).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: Spatial entropy for mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis frames of body masks was significantly higher for White mice (p=0.006, p=0.008, p=0.006, p=0.009 respectively with effect sizes; 2.356, 2.198, 2.370, and 2.132).
source: Comparing the spatial measures between groups of Black and White mice revealed significantly higher spatial entropy for mean, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis frames for White mice (p=0.006, p=0.008, p=0.006, p=0.009 respectively with the following respective effect sizes; 2.356, 2.198, 2.370, and 2.132, Figure 8C).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 8C.

claim: The sharpness of skewness was larger for White mice (p=0.022, effect size = 1.785).
source: The sharpness of skewness was also larger for White mice (p=0.022, effect size = 1.785).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: In the example string pulling epoch, the starting body length is about 40 mm and increases by ~1.5% as the mouse stands and elongates its body.
source: In the example string pulling epoch in the sample video (lasting about eight secs), the starting body length is about 40 mm and increases by ~1.5% as the mouse stands and elongates its body to virtually walk up on the string (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The body tilt remains vertical (between 80°−90°) throughout the epoch.
source: The body tilt however remains vertical (between 80°−90°) throughout the epoch (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Head yaw values are initially greater than 0 and gradually reduce to values less than 0, indicating that the mouse is moving its head from left to right.
source: In the representative string-pulling epoch of the Black mouse, head yaw values are initially greater than 0 and gradually reduce to values less than 0, indicating that the mouse is moving its head from left to right (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: While the mouse pulls the string, the head rolls at a frequency of about three rolls/s.
source: While the mouse pulls the string, the head rolls at a frequency of about three rolls/s (Figure 9F) in the sample video (Video 1).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 9F and Video 1.

claim: The head pitch stays positive most of the time, as the mouse is moving its nose up for sniffing or using its whiskers to track the string.
source: In the sample video, the head pitch stays positive most of the time, as the mouse is moving its nose up for sniffing or using its whiskers to track the string (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 9D with an interpretation.

claim: The nose stays close to the string.
source: Furthermore, as has been previously shown (Blackwell et al., 2018a), the nose stays close to the string (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 9G, supported by a citation to Blackwell et al., 2018a.

claim: The stroke length of pulling is initially shorter and gradually grows for both right and left hands.
source: In the representative epoch of string pulling for the Black mouse, the stroke length of pulling is initially shorter and gradually grows for both right and left hands.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: For the vertical motion, the two hands are alternating, whereas for the horizontal motion, the two hands move to the right and left together.
source: With respect to the common origin, for the vertical motion, the two hands are alternating, whereas for the horizontal motion, the two hands move to the right and left together.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The vertical speed of the hands is about two to three times faster than the horizontal speed.
source: The vertical speed of the hands is about two to three times faster than the horizontal speed.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experimental data.

claim: For each stroke, the rise time (motion from point of release of the string to the point of the grasp) is smaller than the fall time (the time mouse is pulling the string downwards) (Student's t-test, p<0.001, N = 21 cycles).
source: For each stroke, the rise time that is motion from point of release of the string (near the bottom) to the point of the grasp (near the top) is smaller than the fall time which is the time mouse is pulling the string downwards (Student's t-test, p<0.001, N = 21 cycles, Figure 10H).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 10H.

claim: For the horizontal motion, the rise time is larger than the fall time (Student's t-test, p<0.001, N = 22 cycles).
source: For the horizontal motion, however, the strokes are bimodal (Figure 10I), and the rise time is larger than the fall time (Student's t-test, p<0.001, N = 22 cycles, Figure 10J).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data, supported by Figures 10I and 10J.

claim: The White mouse moved the whole body in a rhythmic fashion up and down.
source: Whereas the Black mouse gradually stood up, increasing its body length while pulling, the White mouse moved the whole body in a rhythmic fashion up and down (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 11B.

claim: The White mouse occasionally used its mouth to hold the string.
source: The White mouse occasionally used its mouth to hold the string (Video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from Video 2.

claim: There was no significant difference between maximum body length, minimum body length, and change in body length (max – min) between White and Black mice (Student's t-test, p>0.05).
source: There was no significant difference between maximum body length, minimum body length, and change in body length (max – min) between White and Black mice, Student's t-test, p>0.05.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: Body linear and angular speeds were significantly larger for White compared to Black mice (p=0.0198 and p=0.0199 with effect sizes: 1.837 and 1.834, respectively).
source: However, body linear and angular speeds were significantly larger for White compared to Black mice (p=0.0198 and p=0.0199 with the following effect sizes: 1.837 and 1.834, respectively, Figure 11F).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 11F.

claim: The dominant frequency in body length oscillations was not different between Black and White mice.
source: The dominant frequency in body length oscillations (determined with Fourier transform of the time series of body length) was not different between Black and White mice.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: The dominant frequency of motion for hands was not different between Black and White mice.
source: Similarly, the dominant frequency of motion for hands was not different.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: The peak left-hand vertical speed was slightly significantly larger for White mice (p=0.0445, effect size = 1.506).
source: The peak left-hand vertical speed, however, was slightly significantly larger for White mice (p=0.0445, effect size = 1.506).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data.

claim: Average time of right-hand reach cycles was significantly smaller for White compared to Black mice (p=0.005, effect size = 2.46).
source: Average time of right-hand reach cycles (see examples in Figure 10G) characterized as lift-advance-grasp-pull-push-release (Blackwell et al., 2018a) was significantly smaller for White compared to Black mice (p=0.005, effect size = 2.46) corroborating previous finding that white mice have higher speeds (Figure 11G).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the experimental data, supported by Figures 10G and 11G, and a citation to Blackwell et al., 2018a.

claim: The overall average accuracy for all body parts is ~96%, with higher accuracies for fur and ears compared to those for nose and hands.
source: The overall average accuracy for all body parts is ~96%, with higher accuracies for fur and ears compared to those for nose and hands.
evidence: This is a summary of the accuracy results presented in Table 1.

claim: Errors in hand detection were mostly negligible for the identified position of ears and nose.
source: Errors were mostly negligible for the identified position of ears and nose (Figure 12B,C and F).
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison of heuristic and neural network methods shown in Figure 12.

claim: Errors were up to ~100 pixels (10 mm) for the identification of hands in frames where the speed was large.
source: However, errors were up to ~100 pixels (pix) (10 mm) for the identification of hands in frames where the speed was large (Figure 12A,D and E).
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison of heuristic and neural network methods shown in Figure 12.

claim: Albino mice display anatomical abnormalities in the visual system.
source: It is recognized that albino mice display anatomical abnormalities in the visual system (Lee et al., 2019), other physiological processes for example fatty acid uptake and trafficking (Seeger and Murphy, 2016), and recovery after spinal cord injury (Noristani et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2019, Seeger and Murphy, 2016, and Noristani et al., 2018.

claim: There is evidence that albino strains of laboratory animals display motor system abnormalities.
source: There is also evidence that albino strains of laboratory animals display motor system abnormalities (VandenBerg et al., 2002; Whishaw et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to VandenBerg et al., 2002 and Whishaw et al., 2003.

claim: It is possible that abnormalities in motor systems, such as the corticospinal tracts that control the arms and hands, lead to compensatory whole-body movements of string pulling in the White mice.
source: Thus, it is possible to speculate that abnormalities in motor systems, such as the corticospinal tracts that control the arms and hands, lead to compensatory whole-body movements of string pulling in the White mice, as is reported after motor cortex stroke in mice (Farr and Whishaw, 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results, supported by a citation to Farr and Whishaw, 2002.

claim: The string-pulling procedure captures strain differences in the two exemplar strains of mice.
source: That the string-pulling procedure captures strain differences in the two exemplar strains of mice that are examined, in which Swiss Wister mice display more body motion relative to C57BL/6 mice, shows that the procedures can be used for phenotyping strain differences more generally.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The behavior of string-pulling is homologous to string-pulling described in many other animal species including humans.
source: In addition, the behavior of string-pulling is homologous to string-pulling described in many other animal species including humans, suggesting that our method can be exploited for species comparisons and for developing other animal models of human neurological conditions (Ryait et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ryait et al., 2019 and Singh et al., 2019.

claim: The whole-body analysis approach provides a generic method for analyzing animal behavior.
source: The whole-body analysis approach developed and presented here provides a generic method for analyzing animal behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the method developed in the manuscript.

claim: With the whole-body analysis approach, the need for pose estimation or tracking of body parts is eliminated.
source: With this approach, rather than analyzing kinematics of body movements, overall characteristics of the image sequence and derived spatiotemporal signals such as speed frames are assessed within a spatially confined region representing the average position/location of the animal. Thus, the need for pose estimation or tracking of body parts is eliminated.
evidence: This is a description of the advantages of the whole-body analysis approach.

claim: The success of the heuristic approach to detect body parts automatically is crucially dependent upon the quality of masks generated with image segmentation.
source: The success of the heuristic approach to detect body parts automatically is crucially dependent upon the quality of masks generated with image segmentation.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the heuristic approach.

claim: Machine learning based software for pose estimation such as 'DeepLabCut' and 'Animal Part Tracker' can provide a seamless work flow, but they are computationally intensive initially when training is required.
source: Machine learning (ML) based software for pose estimation in videos such as 'DeepLabCut' (Mathis et al., 2018) and 'Animal Part Tracker' (Kabra et al., 2013) and for object recognition such as 'DeepBehavior' (Arac et al., 2019) can provide a seamless work flow, but they are computationally intensive initially when training is required.
evidence: This is a comparison with other software, supported by citations to Mathis et al., 2018, Kabra et al., 2013, and Arac et al., 2019.

claim: The algorithms presented here are simpler, require smaller computations, and can be implemented on any computer with reasonable computing power.
source: The algorithms presented here are simpler, require smaller computations, and can be implemented on any computer with reasonable computing power and temporary storage for example 2 GHz processor and 32 GB of RAM.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the presented algorithms.

claim: The approach presented here has a faster lead time compared to ML-based methods.
source: The approach presented here also has a faster lead time. The user can obtain results the same day after data acquisition as our software does not need any prior training of a neural network (which can take several days), rather one can open videos and start analyzing right away.
evidence: This is a comparison of the lead time with ML-based methods.

claim: The toolbox is provided under the GNU General Public Licence v3.0, and is open source, free, and any modifications are allowed as long as this paper is cited when publishing or distributing a modified version.
source: This toolbox is provided under the GNU General Public Licence v3.0, and is open source, free, and any modifications are allowed as long as this paper is cited when publishing or distributing a modified version.
evidence: This is a statement about the licensing of the software.

claim: Adult mice 3–6 months old, five male C57 Bl/6J (Black) and five male Swiss Webster Albino (White), were used in this study.
source: Adult mice 3–6 months old, five male C57 Bl/6J (Black) and five male Swiss Webster Albino (White), were used in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The Combined Local-Global (CLG) method was used to estimate optical flow in string pulling videos.
source: The Combined Local-Global (CLG) method was used to estimate optical flow in string pulling videos (Bruhn et al., 2005; Afrashteh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the method used, supported by citations to Bruhn et al., 2005 and Afrashteh et al., 2017.

claim: This method was chosen because it provides a better optical flow estimate compared to Horn-Schunck and Temporospatial methods.
source: This method was chosen because it provides a better optical flow estimate compared to Horn-Schunck and Temporospatial methods (Afrashteh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a justification for the choice of method, supported by a citation to Afrashteh et al., 2017.

claim: A fast independent component analysis (fastICA) algorithm was used to find independent components (ICs) of the image sequence as well as speed frames.
source: A fast independent component analysis (fastICA) algorithm (Hyvärinen and Oja, 2000) was used to find independent components (ICs) of the image sequence as well as speed frames.
evidence: This is a description of the method used, supported by a citation to Hyvärinen and Oja, 2000.

claim: K-means clustering is used to separate colors in the rectangular region into three clusters.
source: K-means clustering is then used to separate colors in the rectangular region into three clusters.
evidence: This is a description of the image segmentation method.

claim: With trial and error, it was found that three clusters were sufficient to separate colors of interest for body and hands while seven clusters were sufficient for separating colors of interest for the string and nose.
source: With trial and error, it was found that three clusters were sufficient to separate colors of interest for body and hands while seven clusters were sufficient for separating colors of interest for the string and nose.
evidence: This is a description of the parameter selection process based on empirical testing.
